How you isolated it (which side you proved innocent first)

Ask one focused question at a time, probe the reasoning behind answers, and give concise Socratic feedback before moving on.

disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Vendor-neutral; not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any framework or platform vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

choices: 200 OK — the request succeeded
201 Created — a new resource was created; pair it with a Location header
204 No Content — creation succeeded but there's nothing to return
200 is fine for creation; status codes don't matter to clients
scenarios.hint: Which status code's definition is literally 'a new resource was created as a result of the request'?
scenarios.prompt: What status should the endpoint return?
scenarios.situation: A POST that creates an order returns 200 OK; the API style guide requires the correct creation semantics.
scenarios.title: The created order that says OK
scenarios.why: 201 Created is the semantic status for successful resource creation, conventionally paired with a Location header pointing at the new resource. 200 means 'here's the result of your request' with no creation implied; 204 means success with intentionally empty body. Status codes are machine-readable contracts — clients, caches, and monitoring all branch on them.

choices: The browser blocks all cross-origin requests — the API must be same-origin
The API's response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and the preflight needs the right Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers) — CORS is enforced by the browser, configured on the server
fetch can't do cross-origin POSTs — use XMLHttpRequest instead
CORS is fixed by adding mode: 'no-cors' — then the response is readable
evidence:
Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/orders' from origin 'https://shop.example.com'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header
scenarios.hint: Who enforces CORS — the server or the browser? And where must the permission be granted?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and where is it fixed?
scenarios.situation: A frontend on shop.example.com can't POST to api.example.com; the console shows a CORS error.
scenarios.title: Blocked by CORS policy
scenarios.why: CORS is a browser-enforced policy: the browser blocks the frontend from reading a cross-origin response unless the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin (plus Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers on the OPTIONS preflight for non-simple requests). The fix is server-side headers, not client workarounds — mode: 'no-cors' makes the response opaque (unreadable). Also: with credentials: 'include', the origin can't be the wildcard *.

choices: GET /getOrders?userId=7 — action verbs in the path are the REST convention
GET /users/7/orders — nested resources express the relationship; filter/sort/paginate via query params
POST /orders/search with the user id in the body — searches should be POSTs
GET /orders with no params — the client filters the full list
evidence: # TODO: endpoint for a user's orders, newest first, 20 per page
scenarios.hint: Resources are nouns, relationships nest, and non-identifying modifiers ride the query string. What identifies the collection here?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic endpoint?
scenarios.situation: An API needs a user's orders, newest first, paginated.
scenarios.title: Designing the orders endpoint
scenarios.why: GET /users/7/orders with ?sort=-created_at&page=2&per_page=20 follows REST conventions: plural nouns, nesting for ownership, query params for filtering/sorting/pagination. Action verbs in paths (getOrders) are RPC style; POST-for-search is for complex bodies; returning everything for client-side filtering doesn't scale. Consistent URL design is a usability feature of the API.

choices: Check response.ok and throw/handle on !ok — fetch only rejects on network failures, not HTTP error statuses
Wrap in try/catch — that catches 404s and 500s automatically
Check response.status === 200 exactly — any other status is an error
fetch rejects on 4xx/5xx — no status handling needed
evidence:
const res = await fetch('/api/orders/9999');
const order = await res.json();  // 404 HTML page -> JSON parse error
scenarios.hint: What does the fetch promise do on a 404 — reject, or resolve with a response whose ok is false?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the 404 become a JSON parse error?
scenarios.situation: Fetching a missing order throws a JSON parse error instead of a clean 'not found'.
scenarios.title: The fetch that doesn't throw
scenarios.why: fetch resolves for any HTTP status — including 404 and 500 — and only rejects on network-level failures (DNS, refused connection). The code must inspect response.ok (or status) before parsing; otherwise a 404 HTML error page goes into .json() and explodes. The pattern: if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...) with the status, then parse.

choices: Send the retry immediately — the server will deduplicate automatically
Send an Idempotency-Key header with a client-generated unique key; the server stores the first result per key and replays it for duplicates
Retries are unsafe and must be disabled for POSTs
Use PUT instead of POST — PUT is idempotent so the problem disappears
evidence:
POST /api/payments -> timeout (unknown: did it charge?)
# client must retry, but a double charge is unacceptable
scenarios.hint: The server can't tell 'retry of the same intent' from 'a second charge'. What client-supplied token lets it distinguish them?
scenarios.prompt: How should the client retry safely?
scenarios.situation: A payment POST times out; the client doesn't know if the charge happened.
scenarios.title: The payment that might have happened
scenarios.why: The Idempotency-Key pattern: the client generates a unique key per intent and sends it on the POST; the server persists the key with the first result and replays that result for subsequent requests with the same key. Retrying blindly risks double-charging; PUT's idempotency only helps if the API is designed around it. For money-moving endpoints, idempotency keys are the industry standard.

choices: Poll the endpoint every second — simple and reliable
Use a webhook: the server POSTs to a client-registered URL when the job completes; verify the signature (HMAC) on receipt
Keep the HTTP connection open for the full 10 minutes — long requests are fine
WebSockets are required — webhooks can't deliver results
scenarios.hint: 202 Accepted means 'received, working on it'. How does the client learn when it's done — without asking forever?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right completion-notification design?
scenarios.situation: An export endpoint returns 202; the client needs the result when the 10-minute job finishes.
scenarios.title: The job that takes ten minutes
scenarios.why: 202 Accepted is the correct immediate response for async work; completion notification belongs to a webhook (server calls the client's registered URL) rather than polling (wasteful) or holding connections open (fragile). The critical companion: verify the webhook signature (HMAC of the payload with a shared secret) so attackers can't forge completion events.

choices: Store the token in a global variable — globals persist across renders
Keep the token in component state (or context) and attach it via an API client wrapper/interceptor that sets the Authorization header on every request
Put the token in the URL query string — headers are unreliable
localStorage is only for strings — tokens must be objects, so it can't be used
evidence: // TODO: attach the JWT to every API call after login
scenarios.hint: Every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. What pattern applies that header in one place instead of at every call site?
scenarios.prompt: How should the token be attached to requests?
scenarios.situation: After login, every API call must carry the JWT.
scenarios.title: The token on every request
scenarios.why: Centralize it: an API client module (or fetch/axios interceptor) reads the stored token and sets Authorization: Bearer on each request. Scattering header logic across call sites guarantees one forgotten call. (Storage choice — memory vs localStorage vs HttpOnly cookie — is a separate XSS-vs-CSRF tradeoff; the attachment pattern is the same.)

choices: Call .json() on the response in the component and pass the parsed object down
Define the expected shape (TypeScript interface or Zod schema) and validate/narrow at the API boundary — fail fast on contract drift
Trust the backend — frontend validation of API shapes is redundant
Use `any` for all API responses — flexibility beats rigidity
evidence:
interface Order { id: number; total: number; }
// API actually returns { id, total, currency } and sometimes total as a string
scenarios.hint: The backend changed its shape and the UI broke silently. Where's the cheapest place to catch 'the shape changed' — at the boundary, or deep in a component?
scenarios.prompt: How should the frontend guard against shape drift?
scenarios.situation: A backend change to the order payload breaks the UI at runtime with no compile-time signal.
scenarios.title: The shape that drifted
scenarios.why: Validate at the boundary: a Zod schema (or careful TypeScript narrowing) on API responses turns silent drift into a loud, early failure at the one place data enters. `any` and blind trust push the breakage deep into components where it's mysterious. Types document the contract; runtime validation enforces it — use both at the seam.

choices: Show a generic 'loading' spinner forever — the request might still succeed
Model the request state explicitly (idle/loading/success/error) and render each state — including the error with a retry action
Errors are rare — render nothing on failure
Reload the whole page on any API error — simplest recovery
evidence:
const [orders, setOrders] = useState(null);
// TODO: loading and error states
scenarios.hint: The UI has three possible realities: waiting, data, failure. How many does it currently render?
scenarios.prompt: What states must the UI handle?
scenarios.situation: An orders page shows a blank screen during load and on failure.
scenarios.title: The blank page
scenarios.why: Every remote-data UI has at least three states — loading, success, error — and users need to see each: skeletons/spinners for loading, data for success, and for errors a message plus a retry action (not a blank page or a forced reload). Explicit state machines (or a data-fetching library's status flags) make the missing states impossible to forget.

choices: Debounce the input at 300ms — fewer requests, problem solved
Cancel the previous request (AbortController) or ignore stale responses — only the latest query's results may render
Cache every response forever — stale data is better than wrong data
Disable the search box while a request is in flight — users must wait
scenarios.hint: Responses arrive out of order. What distinguishes the response you want from the ones you don't — its request?
scenarios.prompt: How do you ensure only the latest results render?
scenarios.situation: Fast typing in a search box shows results for an older query.
scenarios.title: The search that answers late
scenarios.why: Without cancellation, a slow response for 'reac' can land after 'react' and overwrite state — the classic async race. AbortController in the effect cleanup cancels the in-flight request on each keystroke; alternatively, tag responses with the query and ignore mismatches. Debouncing reduces frequency but doesn't fix ordering.

choices: Store the draft in component state and lift it via callbacks (or a tiny store) so navigation preserves it — component state dies with the component
Keep it in the step component's useState — React preserves state across route changes
Store it in the URL hash — hashes survive navigation automatically
Drafts can't survive navigation — warn the user instead
evidence: // 3-step checkout wizard; going Back loses the entered data
scenarios.hint: Route changes unmount the step component. Where does its useState go — and what survives unmounting?
scenarios.prompt: How should the wizard preserve entered data?
scenarios.situation: Going back a step in a checkout wizard wipes the entered data.
scenarios.title: The wizard that forgets
scenarios.why: Component state lives and dies with the component — navigating away unmounts the step and destroys its useState. Lift the draft to a parent that persists across steps (wizard shell state, context, or a small store), or persist to the URL/sessionStorage for refresh-survival. The rule: state must live at least as long as the UI that needs it.

choices: Refetch the list after every mutation — simplest and always correct
Update the local list optimistically (or invalidate the query cache) so the UI reflects the mutation without a full refetch round-trip
Mutations don't affect queries — leave the list stale until the user refreshes
Store the list in a global variable and mutate it directly
scenarios.hint: The mutation succeeded but the query cache doesn't know. What tells the cached list that its data changed?
scenarios.prompt: How should the UI reflect the new todo?
scenarios.situation: After adding a todo, the list doesn't update until a manual refresh.
scenarios.title: The todo that didn't appear
scenarios.why: Mutations and queries are separate cache entries: creating a todo doesn't invalidate the ['todos'] query. The fix is invalidation (queryClient.invalidateQueries(['todos'])) or an optimistic update that inserts the item immediately and rolls back on error. Blind refetching works but wastes a round-trip; optimistic updates make the UI feel instant.

choices: Increase the server timeout to 10 minutes — long requests are fine
Return 202 Accepted immediately with a job id; process in a background worker/queue; let the client poll or receive a webhook on completion
Run the export synchronously but stream the response — streaming fixes timeouts
Tell users to export smaller date ranges — the API is fine
evidence:
POST /api/exports ->504 Gateway Timeout after 60s
# report generation takes ~8 minutes
scenarios.hint: HTTP is a bad home for 8-minute computations. What response says 'accepted, working on it' — and where does the work go?
scenarios.prompt: How should the endpoint be redesigned?
scenarios.situation: A report export takes 8 minutes; the request times out at the gateway.
scenarios.title: The eight-minute request
scenarios.why: Long work doesn't belong in the request lifecycle: gateways, load balancers, and clients all time out. The pattern is 202 Accepted with a job id, a background worker (queue + consumer) doing the work, and completion via polling or webhook. Streaming helps for large-but-fast responses, not for compute-bound minutes.

choices: Validate at the API boundary and reject with 400/422 — never let invalid data reach the domain
Validate in the database with CHECK constraints only — the API should accept anything
Validation is the frontend's job — the API trusts its callers
Catch the database error and return 500 — the client learns from the error
evidence:
// POST /api/bookings accepts { seats: -3, date: "yesterday" }
// -> 500 from a deep service-layer crash
scenarios.hint: The 500 came from deep inside. Where's the earliest point that knows what 'valid' means — and what status tells the client it's their fault?
scenarios.prompt: Where should validation live, and what should the client get?
scenarios.situation: Invalid booking input (negative seats, past date) causes a 500 deep in the service.
scenarios.title: Validation at the wrong layer
scenarios.why: Validate at the API boundary: malformed input is a client error (400/422 with field-level messages), not a server crash. Letting it through to deep layers produces 500s that mislead monitoring and leak internals. Defense in depth adds DB constraints too — but the API contract is enforced at the edge, where the client can act on the feedback.

choices: Log the full card number for debugging — logs are internal
Never handle raw card numbers — use a PCI-compliant processor (Stripe/etc.) with tokenization; card data must never touch your servers/logs
Encrypt the card number in the database — encryption equals compliance
Card data is fine in logs if the log server has a firewall
scenarios.hint: What's the cheapest way to achieve PCI compliance for card data — handle it perfectly, or never touch it at all?
scenarios.prompt: How should card payments be architected?
scenarios.situation: A new checkout needs to process credit cards.
scenarios.title: The card number problem
scenarios.why: The winning move is not to play: tokenization via a compliant processor (Stripe Elements, etc.) means raw PANs never touch your servers, logs, or database — collapsing PCI scope from 'prove everything is secure' to a short SAQ. Encrypting-and-storing keeps the full compliance burden; logging PANs is a breach waiting for an audit.

choices: Log at debug level with full request bodies — more data is better
Log structured events with correlation/request ids, appropriate levels, and no secrets — logs must be searchable and safe
console.log everywhere — structured logging is overkill
Logs are only for errors — successful requests need no logging
evidence:
console.log("user " + userId + " did a thing");
// production incident: can't trace a request across services
scenarios.hint: During an incident you need every log line for one request across three services. What ties them together?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the logging, and what replaces it?
scenarios.situation: An incident can't be traced across services; logs are unstructured strings.
scenarios.title: Logs you can't search
scenarios.why: Structured logging (JSON lines with timestamp, level, service, correlation/request id) makes logs queryable: filter by request id and the whole cross-service trail appears. Unstructured string concatenation can't be filtered or aggregated. Rules: propagate a correlation id through the call chain, pick levels deliberately (debug/info/warn/error), and never log secrets, tokens, or PII.

choices: Deploy the new version to all servers at once — fastest feedback
Roll out gradually (canary a slice of traffic, watch metrics, then proceed) with instant rollback — limit the blast radius of a bad deploy
Deploy on Friday evening — the weekend is quiet for monitoring
Skip staging — production is the real test
evidence: # TODO: release v2.4 of the checkout service
scenarios.hint: If v2.4 has a critical bug, how many users should meet it before you notice — all of them, or a canary slice?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rollout strategy?
scenarios.situation: A checkout service release needs to go out with minimal risk.
scenarios.title: Releasing the checkout
scenarios.why: Canary/blue-green deploys bound the blast radius: route a small percentage to the new version, watch error rates and business metrics, promote or roll back automatically. Big-bang deploys turn every release into an all-or-nothing bet on the busiest service. The rollback path must be as tested as the rollout — 'deploy fast' means 'revert fast'.

choices: Return 500 for every downstream failure — the client's problem
Implement timeouts, retries with backoff (on idempotent calls), and a circuit breaker — fail fast and degrade gracefully instead of cascading
Retry forever until the downstream recovers — persistence pays off
Remove the timeout — waiting longer always resolves it
evidence:
// checkout calls inventory, pricing, and fraud services
// one slow downstream -> all checkout threads pile up -> outage
scenarios.hint: Threads waiting on a hung downstream are threads not serving anyone. What pattern stops calling a service that's clearly down?
scenarios.prompt: How should the service handle downstream failures?
scenarios.situation: A slow inventory service cascades into a full checkout outage.
scenarios.title: The cascade
scenarios.why: Resilience is layered: timeouts bound the wait, retries with exponential backoff + jitter handle transient blips (only on idempotent operations), and the circuit breaker trips after repeated failures — failing fast with a degraded response instead of piling up threads. Without the breaker, one sick dependency takes down every caller: the definition of a cascading failure.

choices: Add an index on every column — indexes are always beneficial
Add an index on (status, created_at) matching the query's filter and sort — then verify with EXPLAIN that it's used
Indexes don't help WHERE clauses — only ORDER BY
Partition the table — indexes can't fix 10M rows
evidence:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50;
-- 8.2s on 10M rows; EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan
scenarios.hint: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What data structure lets the database jump to 'pending' rows in created_at order without reading all 10M?
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix, and how do you confirm it?
scenarios.situation: An orders query takes 8 seconds; EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan.
scenarios.title: The eight-second query
scenarios.why: A composite index on (status, created_at) serves both the equality filter and the ordering from the index, turning 10M-row scans into a targeted range read. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) before and after proves the plan changed. Index-everything is wrong — indexes cost write performance and storage; the right index matches the query's access pattern.

choices: Use SELECT * with a JOIN and deduplicate in code — simplest
JOIN orders to customers and aggregate in SQL (GROUP BY customer) — the database is built for exactly this
Two separate queries and a nested loop in code — avoid JOINs, they're slow
Denormalize everything into one table — joins are a design smell
evidence: -- TODO: revenue per customer for Q3
scenarios.hint: You need one row per customer with a sum. Is that a job for the database's aggregation engine or for application loops?
scenarios.prompt: How should the query be written?
scenarios.situation: Revenue per customer for a quarter is needed from orders and customers tables.
scenarios.title: Revenue per customer
scenarios.why: JOIN + GROUP BY with SUM is the database's home turf: one round-trip, set-based aggregation, the optimizer's choice of hash/sort strategies. Pulling both tables into code for a nested loop ships megabytes to do what the engine does in milliseconds. ('JOINs are slow' is a myth — missing indexes are slow; the join itself is the relational model's core operation.)

choices: Wrap each statement in its own transaction — more transactions equal more safety
Wrap the transfer in a single transaction (BEGIN; debit; credit; COMMIT;) — ACID guarantees both-or-neither
Transactions are automatic — no explicit boundaries needed
Use two connections, one per statement — parallelism is faster
scenarios.hint: A crash between the two UPDATEs destroys money. What boundary makes them atomic?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the transfer atomic?
scenarios.situation: A funds transfer does two UPDATEs; a crash between them loses money.
scenarios.title: The half transfer
scenarios.why: A single transaction makes the debit+credit atomic: either both commit or neither does (with rollback on failure) — the A in ACID. Autocommit mode commits each statement separately, which is exactly the money-destroying behavior. Explicit BEGIN/COMMIT (or the driver's transaction block) is the unit of consistency for multi-statement operations.

choices: Store the tags as a comma-separated string in the product row — one table, simple
A junction table product_tags(product_id, tag_id) with foreign keys — the normalized many-to-many
A JSON array column of tag names — flexible and queryable
One boolean column per tag — explicit and fast
evidence: -- products can have many tags; tags apply to many products
scenarios.hint: Many-to-many with attributes on neither side alone. Which relational structure represents 'pairs' without duplication?
scenarios.prompt: How should the schema model it?
scenarios.situation: Products and tags are many-to-many; the schema is undecided.
scenarios.title: Products, tags, and pairs
scenarios.why: A junction table with two foreign keys (composite primary key) is the normalized many-to-many: no duplication, referential integrity both ways, and room for relationship attributes (tagged_at). Comma-separated strings break querying and integrity; JSON columns are fine for schemaless payloads but lose FK guarantees; boolean-per-tag doesn't scale. Normalization isn't dogma — it's the structure that prevents update anomalies.

choices: Run migrations explicitly as a deploy step (migrate before the new code serves) — schema and code stay in lockstep
Edit the production schema by hand when needed — fastest
Let the ORM auto-migrate on startup (sync) — automation handles it
Migrations are only for development — production schemas are managed separately
scenarios.hint: The new code expects the new column. If the code deploys before the column exists, what happens on the first request?
scenarios.prompt: How should schema changes ship?
scenarios.situation: A deploy needs a new column; the pipeline has no migration step.
scenarios.title: Code without its column
scenarios.why: Migrations run as an explicit deploy step before the new code takes traffic — the schema the code was written against must exist when it runs. Hand-editing production drifts untracked; ORM auto-sync on startup races across instances and can destroy data. For zero-downtime, expand-then-contract (add column, deploy, backfill, then remove) — but the baseline is: migrate, then serve.

choices: Relational for everything — NoSQL is a fad
A document store for the catalog (flexible, read-heavy product data) and relational for orders/inventory (transactions, integrity) — match the store to the access pattern
Key-value for everything — simplest model
The team should only ever use one database — polyglot persistence is unmaintainable
evidence:
# catalog: 2M products, flexible attributes, read-heavy
# orders: money movement, strict integrity
scenarios.hint: One workload needs flexible schemas and fast reads; the other needs ACID and joins. Must one database serve both?
scenarios.prompt: How should the data be split?
scenarios.situation: A platform has a read-heavy flexible catalog and transactional order data.
scenarios.title: One database or two?
scenarios.why: Polyglot persistence matches stores to workloads: a document store fits the catalog's flexible, read-heavy shape; the relational database fits orders' transactional integrity (ACID, joins, constraints). One-database dogma forces one workload into the wrong model. The cost — two systems to operate — is real, so the split must earn it: here the access patterns genuinely differ.

choices: MD5(password) — fast and simple
bcrypt/argon2 with per-password salts — adaptive, slow hashes that resist brute force
SHA-256 with a site-wide salt — one salt is enough
Base64-encode the password — encoding obscures it
scenarios.hint: GPUs try billions of hashes per second. What property must the hash function have to make each guess expensive?
scenarios.prompt: How should passwords be stored?
scenarios.situation: A new auth system needs password storage.
scenarios.title: Storing passwords, again
scenarios.why: Adaptive hashes (bcrypt, argon2, scrypt) are deliberately slow and salted per password — each guess costs real time, defeating GPU brute force, and salts defeat rainbow tables. Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256) fall in hours; a site-wide salt still allows parallel attacks; encoding is not hashing. The work factor should rise as hardware improves.

choices: Decode the JWT payload and trust the role claim — the signature is optional
Verify the signature with the server's secret/key, check exp, then trust the claims — an unverified JWT is just a suggestion
JWTs can't carry roles — use a database lookup for every request
Accept any JWT with three dot-separated parts — structure implies validity
scenarios.hint: The payload is just base64 — anyone can mint one. What part proves the server issued it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the vulnerability?
scenarios.situation: An API trusts the JWT role claim without verifying the signature.
scenarios.title: The self-issued admin token
scenarios.why: A JWT's payload is merely base64-encoded — anyone can craft {"role":"admin"}. Security comes entirely from verifying the signature (HMAC secret or public key) and checking exp/nbf/aud. Skipping verification turns the token into a client assertion. Rule: never trust claims from an unverified token; verify first, then read.

choices: A 30-day access token in localStorage — simple and long-lived
A short-lived access token (minutes) plus a rotating refresh token stored securely — compromise windows stay small
No tokens — HTTP Basic on every request
One permanent token per user, never expiring — rotation is complexity
evidence: # TODO: token lifetimes for the SPA
scenarios.hint: If an access token leaks, how long is it useful? What bounds that window — and how does the client get a new one silently?
scenarios.prompt: What is the sound token strategy?
scenarios.situation: A single-page app needs an auth token strategy.
scenarios.title: How long should a token live?
scenarios.why: Short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) bound the damage of a leak; rotating refresh tokens (single-use, replaced on each use, theft-detecting) let the client silently obtain new ones. Long-lived bearer tokens are bearer-everything — whoever holds them is the user for weeks. Rotation adds theft detection: reuse of a spent refresh token signals compromise and revokes the family.

choices: localStorage — JavaScript needs to read the token
A cookie with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax/Strict — HttpOnly keeps it out of JavaScript's reach (XSS can't steal what it can't read)
A cookie with no flags — flags are optional hardening
The token in the page's HTML — simplest
scenarios.hint: XSS runs JavaScript in your page. What storage keeps the token away from JavaScript entirely — and what new risk does cookie storage introduce?
scenarios.prompt: Where should the session token live?
scenarios.situation: The team debates localStorage vs cookies for the session token.
scenarios.title: Where does the token live?
scenarios.why: HttpOnly cookies are invisible to JavaScript, so XSS can't exfiltrate the token — localStorage offers no such protection. The tradeoff: cookies are sent automatically, so CSRF protection (SameSite + anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests) becomes mandatory. There's no risk-free option — only a chosen tradeoff: HttpOnly cookie + CSRF defense is the standard for session auth.

choices: Collect and store user passwords — you need them to verify identity
Use OAuth2 authorization code flow (with PKCE for SPAs): redirect to the provider, get a code, exchange it server-side for tokens — your app never sees the password
Ask users for their Google password and validate it against Google
OAuth is only for social logins — enterprise SSO can't use it
evidence: # TODO: 'Sign in with Google' for the SaaS app
scenarios.hint: Who should ever see the user's Google password — Google, or your app too?
scenarios.prompt: How should third-party login be implemented?
scenarios.situation: A SaaS app needs 'Sign in with Google'.
scenarios.title: Signing in with Google
scenarios.why: The authorization code flow delegates credential handling to the provider: the user authenticates with Google, your app receives a one-time code, and your server exchanges it (with client secret, never exposed) for tokens. Your app never touches the password. PKCE secures the flow for public clients (SPAs) that can't keep a secret. Storing or proxying provider passwords defeats the entire purpose.

choices: Log the user out everywhere on password change and rotate session ids on privilege change — sessions must be revocable server-side
Sessions can't be revoked — that's why JWTs are better
Store the session in a JWT so logout is client-side
Session ids never need rotation — they're random enough

// sessions stored server-side in Redis, id in HttpOnly cookie
// TODO: logout and password-change semantics
scenarios.hint: The session record lives in your Redis. What does deleting it accomplish — and when should the id itself change?
scenarios.prompt: How should logout and password change work?
scenarios.situation: Server-side sessions need logout and password-change semantics.
scenarios.title: Killing a session
scenarios.why: Server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation: delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work. Rotate the session id on login and privilege escalation to prevent fixation. (This revocability is exactly what stateless JWTs lack — hence short lifetimes and denylists there.)

choices: Run tests manually before pushing — CI is overhead
A workflow triggered on push/PR that installs, lints, tests, and builds — every change gets the same checks automatically
CI should only run nightly — per-push runs waste minutes
Commit directly to main and test in production — fastest feedback

scenarios.hint: What breaks when checks are manual — consistency, or speed? What does the pipeline guarantee about every PR?
scenarios.prompt: What does the pipeline buy the team?
scenarios.situation: A team debates adding CI; currently tests run manually 'when someone remembers'.
scenarios.title: The pipeline that remembers
scenarios.why: CI makes verification automatic and uniform: every push and PR gets the same install/lint/test/build sequence, so 'it passed on my machine' becomes 'it passed the pipeline'. Manual testing decays under deadline pressure; per-PR automation catches breakage at the smallest possible diff. The workflow file is versioned with the code — the checks evolve with the project.

choices: Commit the key to the repo — the repo is private
Store it in the CI secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, etc.) and reference via env — secrets never live in source
Paste it into the workflow logs for debugging — logs are internal
Email it to the team — everyone needs it
scenarios.hint: The workflow needs the key but the repo is cloned everywhere. Where can the runner read it without it living in git?
scenarios.prompt: How should the deploy key be provided?
scenarios.situation: A deploy workflow needs a production API key.
scenarios.title: The key in the pipeline
scenarios.why: CI secret stores inject secrets as environment variables at runtime — masked in logs, never in git history. Committed secrets leak to every clone, fork, and CI log forever (and key rotation becomes archaeology). The rule is absolute: secrets enter through the environment, never through source.

choices: One Dockerfile stage that installs everything — simplest to read
Multi-stage: a build stage (SDK, dev deps) compiles the app, then a slim runtime stage copies only the built output — small, fast, attack-surface-minimal images
Docker images should include the full OS toolchain for debugging
Skip Docker — deploy the raw binaries

FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./

CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
scenarios.hint: The final image only needs to RUN the app, not build it. What rides along if you ship the build stage — compilers, dev deps, source?
scenarios.prompt: Why the two stages?
scenarios.situation: A Dockerfile uses a build stage and a slim runtime stage.
scenarios.title: Two stages, one image
scenarios.why: Multi-stage builds separate concerns: the build stage has the SDK and dev dependencies to compile; the runtime stage copies only the built artifact plus production deps. Result: smaller images (faster pulls/deploys), fewer vulnerabilities (no compilers in prod), and no source leakage. Single-stage images ship the entire toolchain to production.

choices: TLS is optional for internal tools — skip it
Terminate TLS at the reverse proxy/load balancer with a managed certificate (Let's Encrypt) — plaintext HTTP only inside the private network
Each app server manages its own certificate manually — full control
TLS slows everything down — disable it for performance

scenarios.situation: A public app currently serves plain HTTP.

scenarios.why: TLS terminates at the edge (reverse proxy/load balancer) with automatically renewed certificates — one place to manage the lifecycle instead of N app servers. Unencrypted public HTTP leaks credentials and content to every network observer.

choices: The homepage returning 200 — if it loads, the app is fine
A dedicated /health endpoint checking dependencies (DB, cache) with 200/503 semantics — the load balancer's routing decision needs the real signal

scenarios.situation: An orchestrator needs to know whether the API can serve traffic.
scenarios.title: Healthy process, sick app

choices: Build once, configure per environment via env vars — the same artifact runs everywhere

Configure via code branches per environment — #if PROD

scenarios.prompt: How should environment differences be handled?

lessons.title: HTTP & APIs — Core concepts
concepts: Status codes are machine-readable contracts — clients, caches, and monitoring all branch on them. fetch resolves for any HTTP status — including 404 and 500 — and only rejects on network-level failures (DNS, refused connection).
REST: GET /users/7/orders with ?sort=-created_at&page=2&per_page=20 follows REST conventions: plural nouns, nesting for ownership, query params for filtering/sorting/pagination.

CORS is a browser-enforced policy: the browser blocks the frontend from reading a cross-origin response unless the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin (plus Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers on the OPTIONS preflight for non-simple requests).
REST design: consistent URL design is a usability feature of the API.
Resource modeling: 201 Created is the semantic status for successful resource creation, conventionally paired with a Location header pointing at the new resource.

example.code:
const res = await fetch('/api/orders/9999');
const order = await res.json();  // 404 HTML page -> JSON parse error
example.walkthrough: fetch resolves for any HTTP status — including 404 and 500 — and only rejects on network-level failures (DNS, refused connection). The code must inspect response.ok (or status) before parsing; otherwise a 404 HTML error page goes into .json() and explodes. The pattern: if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...) with the status, then parse.

pitfalls: Common trap: 200 is fine for creation; status codes don't matter to clients.
Common trap: the API's response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and the preflight needs the right Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers).
Common trap: CORS is fixed by adding mode: 'no-cors'.
Common trap: action verbs in the path are the REST convention.

lessons.title: Frontend Integration — Core concepts
concepts: API clients: centralize it: an API client module (or fetch/axios interceptor) reads the stored token and sets Authorization: Bearer on each request.

Validation: types document the contract; runtime validation enforces it — use both at the seam. Fix it by invalidation (queryClient.invalidateQueries(['todos'])) or an optimistic update that inserts the item immediately and rolls back on error.

UI states: every remote-data UI has at least three states — loading, success, error — and users need to see each: skeletons/spinners for loading, data for success, and for errors a message plus a retry action (not a blank page or a forced reload).

example.code:
interface Order { id: number; total: number; }
// API actually returns { id, total, currency } and sometimes total as a string
example.walkthrough: Validate at the boundary: a Zod schema (or careful TypeScript narrowing) on API responses turns silent drift into a loud, early failure at the one place data enters. `any` and blind trust push the breakage deep into components where it's mysterious. Types document the contract; runtime validation enforces it — use both at the seam.

pitfalls: Common trap: frontend validation of API shapes is redundant.
Common trap: reload the whole page on any API error.
Common trap: define the expected shape (TypeScript interface or Zod schema) and validate/narrow at the API boundary.
Common trap: cancel the previous request (AbortController) or ignore stale responses.

lessons.title: Backend Services — Core concepts
concepts: 202 Accepted: the pattern: 202 Accepted with a job id, a background worker (queue + consumer) doing the work, and completion via polling or webhook.

PCI: the winning move is not to play: tokenization via a compliant processor (Stripe Elements, etc.) means raw PANs never touch your servers, logs, or database — collapsing PCI scope from 'prove everything is secure' to a short SAQ.
Principle: long work doesn't belong in the request lifecycle: gateways, load balancers, and clients all time out.

example.code:
// checkout calls inventory, pricing, and fraud services
// one slow downstream -> all checkout threads pile up -> outage
example.walkthrough: Resilience is layered: timeouts bound the wait, retries with exponential backoff + jitter handle transient blips (only on idempotent operations), and the circuit breaker trips after repeated failures — failing fast with a degraded response instead of piling up threads. Without the breaker, one sick dependency takes down every caller: the definition of a cascading failure.

pitfalls: Common trap: roll out gradually (canary a slice of traffic, watch metrics, then proceed) with instant rollback.
Common trap: card data is fine in logs if the log server has a firewall.
Common trap: tell users to export smaller date ranges.
Common trap: log at debug level with full request bodies.

lessons.title: Databases — Core concepts
concepts: Indexes: ('JOINs are slow' is a myth — missing indexes are slow; the join itself is the relational model's core operation.). Index-everything is wrong — indexes cost write performance and storage; the right index matches the query's access pattern.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) before and after proves the plan changed.

JOINs: polyglot persistence matches stores to workloads: a document store fits the catalog's flexible, read-heavy shape; the relational database fits orders' transactional integrity (ACID, joins, constraints).
Aggregation: JOIN + GROUP BY with SUM is the database's home turf: one round-trip, set-based aggregation, the optimizer's choice of hash/sort strategies.
ACID: a single transaction makes the debit+credit atomic: either both commit or neither does (with rollback on failure) — the A in ACID.

example.code: -- products can have many tags; tags apply to many products
example.walkthrough: A junction table with two foreign keys (composite primary key) is the normalized many-to-many: no duplication, referential integrity both ways, and room for relationship attributes (tagged_at). Comma-separated strings break querying and integrity; JSON columns are fine for schemaless payloads but lose FK guarantees; boolean-per-tag doesn't scale. Normalization isn't dogma — it's the structure that prevents update anomalies.

pitfalls: Common trap: wrap the transfer in a single transaction (BEGIN; debit; credit; COMMIT;).
Common trap: JOIN orders to customers and aggregate in SQL (GROUP BY customer).
Common trap: two separate queries and a nested loop in code.
Common trap: store the tags as a comma-separated string in the product row.

lessons.title: Auth & Sessions — Core concepts
concepts: Password storage: server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation: delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work.
JWT: a JWT's payload is merely base64-encoded — anyone can craft {"role":"admin"}. (This revocability is exactly what stateless JWTs lack — hence short lifetimes and denylists there.).
Signature verification: security comes entirely from verifying the signature (HMAC secret or public key) and checking exp/nbf/aud.
Token lifetimes: rotation adds theft detection: reuse of a spent refresh token signals compromise and revokes the family. Skipping verification turns the token into a client assertion.
Refresh rotation: short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) bound the damage of a leak; rotating refresh tokens (single-use, replaced on each use, theft-detecting) let the client silently obtain new ones.

example.code:
// sessions stored server-side in Redis, id in HttpOnly cookie

example.walkthrough: Server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation: delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work. Rotate the session id on login and privilege escalation to prevent fixation.

pitfalls: Common trap: verify the signature with the server's secret/key, check exp, then trust the claims.
Common trap: ask users for their Google password and validate it against Google.
Common trap: accept any JWT with three dot-separated parts.
Common trap: one permanent token per user, never expiring.

Secrets management: committed secrets leak to every clone, fork, and CI log forever (and key rotation becomes archaeology).
TLS terminates at the edge (reverse proxy/load balancer) with automatically renewed certificates — one place to manage the lifecycle instead of N app servers.

The homepage 200 lies when the DB is down; log scraping isn't a signal. Distinguish liveness (is it running) from readiness (can it serve).

lessons.title: Full-Stack Development — Core concepts
concepts: REST is a contract about resources and semantics: URLs name things, verbs (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) declare intent, and idempotency (PUT/DELETE safe to repeat) lets clients retry without fear.

Never trust the client. Validate and authorize on the server for every request — the browser is a hostile environment, and anything stored where JavaScript can read it (localStorage) is readable by injected script too.

Authentication answers 'who are you', authorization answers 'what can you do'. Short-lived access tokens plus rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection give strong sessions without constant re-login.
The database and the code deploy as a unit: during rolling deploys old and new code coexist, so migrations must be additive first (expand), code second, cleanup last (contract).

Architecture follows team and scale pain, not fashion. A modular monolith with real boundaries beats premature microservices; extract a service when ownership or independent scaling demands it, not before.
Observability is a feature: structured logs, request tracing, and APM turn 'the API is slow' into a flame graph pointing at the exact N+1 query or cold cache.

example.code:
curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/users/42/preferences \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"email":true,"sms":false}' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'
# expect 200; repeat the identical call → still 200, same end state (idempotent)
example.walkthrough: PUT replaces the whole preferences document at the user-scoped URL. Repeating the identical request is safe by design — that idempotency is what lets clients and load balancers retry confidently.

pitfalls: Common trap: using POST for everything — you lose idempotency semantics and make retries dangerous; match the verb to the operation.
Common trap: authorizing once at login and trusting a role claim in the token forever — re-check authorization per request, especially for destructive actions.
Common trap: running migrations after the new code is live — during rolling deploys the new code hits the old schema; migrate first, code second.
Common trap: caching to hide an N+1 instead of fixing the query — the cache masks the shape problem and adds invalidation bugs on top.

simulations.title: The CORS error
simulations.brief: The frontend at app.example.com calls api.example.com and the browser blocks every request: 'CORS policy: No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header'.

steps.symptom: Browser console shows CORS errors; the same API works fine from curl.
evidence: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy.
options: Recognize the split: curl has no origin policy, browsers enforce it — the API must send CORS headers for the frontend's origin
steps.explain: curl proves the API is healthy; the browser's same-origin policy is doing its job. The fix belongs on the server: declare which origins may call it.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: missing CORS headers on API responses.
evidence: app.use(cors());  // no options — reflects nothing specific
options: Configure CORS explicitly: allow https://app.example.com (and only it), with the methods and headers the app needs
Proxy everything through the frontend server
Tell users to install a CORS extension
steps.explain: Explicit allowlisting is the fix: the exact origin, the methods used, and credentials only if the app needs cookies. Wildcard-plus-credentials is forbidden by the spec.

steps.symptom: Fix applied. Verify from the browser's perspective.
options: Confirm the header is present on real responses and the frontend loads data without console errors
Confirm the header appears on 404s too
steps.explain: The header on a real response plus a clean console is the proof — curl can't verify CORS because curl never enforces it.

simulations.debrief: CORS errors are server-config issues wearing a browser's uniform. Allowlist the exact origin, never wildcard with credentials, and verify in the browser — not curl.

simulations.title: HTTP request lifecycle
simulations.brief: Restore the order of a full HTTP request lifecycle.

steps.context: Arrange the stages from URL to response.
items: DNS resolves the hostname to an IP
TCP handshake opens the connection
TLS handshake secures it (for https)
Client sends the HTTP request
Server returns the HTTP response

simulations.debrief: DNS → TCP → TLS → request → response. Each stage has its own failure mode — and its own debugging tool.

simulations.title: Cookie or token?
simulations.brief: Choose the session mechanism for two clients of the same API.

steps.text: Client 1 is a server-rendered web app on the same domain. Mechanism?

choices.label: HttpOnly cookie session: automatic, CSRF-protected, revocable server-side
choices.feedback: Right: same-domain web apps are the home turf of cookie sessions.

choices.label: JWT in localStorage
choices.feedback: localStorage is XSS-readable; HttpOnly cookies are not.

choices.label: API key in the URL
choices.feedback: Keys in URLs leak into logs, history, and referers.

steps.text: Client 2 is a CLI tool scripting the API. Mechanism?

choices.label: Long-lived API token in the Authorization header, scoped and revocable
choices.feedback: Right: CLIs can't do cookie flows well — scoped tokens are the convention.

choices.label: The user's password on every call
choices.feedback: Passwords on every call maximize exposure and can't be scoped or revoked granularly.

choices.label: No auth — it's just a script
choices.feedback: Client type never determines auth need.

simulations.debrief: Same-domain web → cookie sessions; programmatic clients → scoped tokens. Match the mechanism to the client's constraints.

simulations.title: The .env that misfires
simulations.brief: The service crashes on boot reading its environment. .env has 2 bugs in 8 lines.

steps.config:
PORT=eighty
DATABASE_URL=localhost:5432/shop
NODE_ENV=production
LOG_LEVEL=info
SESSION_SECRET=dev-secret
# start: npm start
# health: GET /health

issues.description: PORT=eighty is not a number — the server can't listen on it and crashes parsing the value.
issues.fix: Set PORT=3000 (or another valid port number).

issues.description: DATABASE_URL is missing its scheme (postgres://) — the client library can't parse a bare host:port/path.

simulations.debrief: Env files are untyped: a word where a port belongs and a missing URL scheme both crash the boot. Validate env at startup and fail with a clear message.

consoleSims.title: Fix the fetch URL in the IDE
consoleSims.brief: api.js calls the wrong host — requests go to localhost in production. Fix the base URL in the IDE.

tasks.instruction: Open api.js in the code editor.
tasks.hint: Find api.js in the file explorer.

tasks.instruction: Change line 3 to use the API_BASE_URL environment variable.
tasks.hint: Never hardcode hosts — read them from the environment.

tasks.instruction: Run the debugger and confirm requests target the right host.
tasks.hint: Use the Run and Debug control.

consoleSims.debrief: Hardcoded hosts are deployment bugs waiting to happen. Environment variables make the same build run everywhere.

consoleSims.title: Rerun the failed deploy stage
consoleSims.brief: The pipeline failed at 'deploy' after 'build' and 'test' passed. Fix the PORT variable and rerun.

tasks.instruction: Open the failed 'deploy' stage in the pipeline view.

tasks.hint: The stage failed because PORT was not a number.

tasks.instruction: Rerun the deploy stage and confirm it goes green.
tasks.hint: Use the rerun control on the deploy stage.

consoleSims.debrief: Build-green/deploy-red with a bad PORT means the artifact was fine and the environment was wrong. Fix the variable, rerun the stage.

sections.heading: HTTP & APIs
items: Status codes are machine-readable contracts — clients, caches, and monitoring all branch on them. fetch resolves for any HTTP status — including 404 and 500 — and only rejects on network-level failures (DNS, refused connection).
REST — GET /users/7/orders with ?sort=-created_at&page=2&per_page=20 follows REST conventions: plural nouns, nesting for ownership, query params for filtering/sorting/pagination.

CORS is a browser-enforced policy — the browser blocks the frontend from reading a cross-origin response unless the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin (plus Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers on the OPTIONS preflight for non-simple requests).
REST design — consistent URL design is a usability feature of the API.
Resource modeling — 201 Created is the semantic status for successful resource creation, conventionally paired with a Location header pointing at the new resource.
Common trap — 200 is fine for creation; status codes don't matter to clients.
Common trap — the API's response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and the preflight needs the right Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers).
Common trap — CORS is fixed by adding mode: 'no-cors'.
Common trap — action verbs in the path are the REST convention.

sections.heading: Frontend Integration
items: API clients — centralize it: an API client module (or fetch/axios interceptor) reads the stored token and sets Authorization: Bearer on each request.

Validation — types document the contract; runtime validation enforces it — use both at the seam. Fix it by invalidation (queryClient.invalidateQueries(['todos'])) or an optimistic update that inserts the item immediately and rolls back on error.

UI states — every remote-data UI has at least three states — loading, success, error — and users need to see each: skeletons/spinners for loading, data for success, and for errors a message plus a retry action (not a blank page or a forced reload).
Common trap — frontend validation of API shapes is redundant.
Common trap — reload the whole page on any API error.
Common trap — define the expected shape (TypeScript interface or Zod schema) and validate/narrow at the API boundary.

items: 202 Accepted — the pattern: 202 Accepted with a job id, a background worker (queue + consumer) doing the work, and completion via polling or webhook.

PCI — the winning move is not to play: tokenization via a compliant processor (Stripe Elements, etc.) means raw PANs never touch your servers, logs, or database — collapsing PCI scope from 'prove everything is secure' to a short SAQ.
Principle — long work doesn't belong in the request lifecycle: gateways, load balancers, and clients all time out.
Common trap — roll out gradually (canary a slice of traffic, watch metrics, then proceed) with instant rollback.
Common trap — card data is fine in logs if the log server has a firewall.
Common trap — tell users to export smaller date ranges.
Common trap — log at debug level with full request bodies.

sections.heading: Databases
items: Indexes — ('JOINs are slow' is a myth — missing indexes are slow; the join itself is the relational model's core operation.). Index-everything is wrong — indexes cost write performance and storage; the right index matches the query's access pattern.
EXPLAIN — EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) before and after proves the plan changed.

JOINs — polyglot persistence matches stores to workloads: a document store fits the catalog's flexible, read-heavy shape; the relational database fits orders' transactional integrity (ACID, joins, constraints).
Aggregation — JOIN + GROUP BY with SUM is the database's home turf: one round-trip, set-based aggregation, the optimizer's choice of hash/sort strategies.
ACID — a single transaction makes the debit+credit atomic: either both commit or neither does (with rollback on failure) — the A in ACID.
Common trap — wrap the transfer in a single transaction (BEGIN; debit; credit; COMMIT;).
Common trap — JOIN orders to customers and aggregate in SQL (GROUP BY customer).
Common trap — two separate queries and a nested loop in code.
Common trap — store the tags as a comma-separated string in the product row.

sections.heading: Auth & Sessions
items: Password storage — server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation: delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work.
JWT — a JWT's payload is merely base64-encoded — anyone can craft {"role":"admin"}. (This revocability is exactly what stateless JWTs lack — hence short lifetimes and denylists there.).
Signature verification — security comes entirely from verifying the signature (HMAC secret or public key) and checking exp/nbf/aud.
Token lifetimes — rotation adds theft detection: reuse of a spent refresh token signals compromise and revokes the family. Skipping verification turns the token into a client assertion.

Refresh rotation — short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) bound the damage of a leak; rotating refresh tokens (single-use, replaced on each use, theft-detecting) let the client silently obtain new ones.
Common trap — verify the signature with the server's secret/key, check exp, then trust the claims.
Common trap — ask users for their Google password and validate it against Google.
Common trap — accept any JWT with three dot-separated parts.
Common trap — one permanent token per user, never expiring.

Server-side sessions' superpower is instant revocation — delete the Redis record and the session dies everywhere — logout, password change, and 'sign out all devices' all work. Rotate the session id on login and privilege escalation to prevent fixation.

items: CI: multi-stage builds separate concerns — the build stage has the SDK and dev dependencies to compile; the runtime stage copies only the built artifact plus production deps. CI secret stores inject secrets as environment variables at runtime — masked in logs, never in git history.
Secrets management — committed secrets leak to every clone, fork, and CI log forever (and key rotation becomes archaeology).
TLS — TLS terminates at the edge (reverse proxy/load balancer) with automatically renewed certificates — one place to manage the lifecycle instead of N app servers.
Common trap — store it in the CI secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, etc.) and reference via env.
Common trap — terminate TLS at the reverse proxy/load balancer with a managed certificate (Let's Encrypt).
Common trap — docker images should include the full OS toolchain for debugging.
Common trap — TLS is optional for internal tools.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For HTTP & APIs: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Frontend Integration lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Backend Services terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
